content: The qualitative study did not provide conclusive evidence on whether goggles and face shields are equivalent in terms of their effectiveness. The data compared wearing goggles under versus over head-and-neck skin coverings but did not include studies on cost-effectiveness. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) concluded that the cost-effectiveness of wearing goggles under or over the head-and-neck skin covering does not favor either option. In a mixed-methods study, 12% of participants expressed equity concerns, 52% had no equity concerns, and 36% were unsure. Groups identified as having reduced access included individuals who wear glasses or hearing aids, certain ethnic groups (e.g., Muslim women, reverend sisters), and women with long hair. The GDG determined that wearing goggles under versus over the head-and-neck skin covering likely has no impact on health equity. Regarding acceptability, 12% of participants found wearing eye protection under the head-and-neck covering less acceptable, and another 12% found it probably less acceptable. Conversely, 14% found it probably more acceptable, 35% found it more acceptable, 14% indicated it varied, and 14% were unsure. Among the 49% who found wearing eye protection under the covering more or probably more acceptable, reasons included better protection of mucous membranes and the ability to remove eye protection last. Those who found it less or probably less acceptable cited discomfort and the ease of removing eye protection worn over the covering. Participants who indicated variability believed acceptability depended on the type of eye protection used (goggles versus face shields) and the availability of resources like anti-fog formulations. Consistency in practice was also considered important. The GDG judged that wearing eye protection over or under the head-and-neck covering was equally acceptable. A non-comparative simulation study and a consensus panel in the UK provided contextual data on feasibility. No contamination events were reported during a video exercise involving a unified PPE ensemble with a disposable full-face visor worn over the hood. In an online survey, 45% of participants found it more or probably more feasible to wear eye protection under the head-and-neck covering, 35% found it less or probably less feasible, and 9% said it varied. Reasons for greater feasibility included alignment with training and current practice, as well as ease of use. Reasons for reduced feasibility included challenges in adjusting face shields or goggles under the hood, distortion of the shield, and unclear vision. Participants who indicated variability noted that feasibility depended on the type of eye protection used, with goggles being more feasible under the covering and face shields less so. The GDG concluded that wearing eye protection under or over the head-and-neck covering was equally feasible. The GDG discussed whether a recommendation should be made regarding wearing eye protection under or over the head-and-neck covering. The 2014 recommendations were made without a systematic review of data, but the 2022 systematic review provided no evidence to resolve this question. While some members considered abstaining from making a recommendation, the importance of recommendations for training and educational materials was emphasized. Field experience since 2014, including variations in practice, was also discussed. The GDG issued a conditional recommendation in favor of wearing eye protection under the head-and-neck covering, provided it was feasible with the available PPE. For gloves, nitrile gloves are preferred over latex due to their resistance to chemicals, including disinfectants like chlorine, and their lower environmental impact. Latex gloves are associated with a high rate of allergies and contact dermatitis among healthcare workers, with up to 12% experiencing reactions such as skin irritation, itching, burning, and allergic symptoms. If nitrile gloves are unavailable, non-powdered latex gloves may be used, as powdered gloves can cause sensitivity and environmental contamination. Outer gloves should reach mid-forearm (minimum 280 mm total length) to prevent exposure to fluids. This recommendation is based on moderate-certainty evidence and aligns with health worker preferences. For protective bodywear, the choice between disposable gowns and aprons or disposable coveralls and aprons should be based on fabric tested for resistance to penetration by blood, body fluids, or bloodborne pathogens. Gowns are generally more comfortable for limited physical activity and culturally appropriate in certain settings, while coveralls allow easier movement but may pose a higher risk of heat stress. The GDG found no comparative evidence on the effectiveness of gowns versus coveralls in reducing filovirus transmission. Both were deemed equally acceptable, and the choice should depend on availability and health worker preference. Implementation considerations include training, quality criteria, protocols for reuse or disposal, and addressing potential confusion due to varying organizational preferences for different types of coveralls. Survey participants reported low or very low perceived risk of transmission regardless of the type of gown worn. Communication and patient care were more frequently impaired with coveralls than with impermeable gowns. Personal well-being, including heat stress and dehydration, varied among health workers for both coveralls and gowns.
